records.sourceFile: Pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies for enhancing sleep quality in athletes - Implications for performance and recovery.pdf

paper.citation: Tymińska P, Frączek J, Borówka K, Donocik W, Górka P, Kawka N. Pharmacological and Non-Pharmacological Strategies for Enhancing Sleep Quality in Athletes: Implications for Performance and Recovery. Quality in Sport. 2025;41:60176.
paper.abstract: This review describes the physiology of sleep in athletes, the multifactorial causes of insomnia (overtraining, evening workouts, jet lag, pre-event stress, injury and metabolic disease), and pharmacological options including melatonin, non-benzodiazepine hypnotics, cannabidiol and certain antidepressants. The authors conclude that pharmacotherapy may give short-term benefit in select situations, while CBT-I remains the gold standard for long-term management, and that an integrated, personalized approach offers the greatest potential.
paper.tldr: Sleep problems in athletes often come from training timing, travel, stress and overtraining. Behavioural treatment, especially CBT-I, is the preferred long-term approach, and medications are short-term options that need medical oversight and tested products.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The paper does not describe a literature search, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal. It draws on physiology, sleep medicine and sports science references.
paper.findings: The review states that sleep disturbance is common in athletes and that evening high-intensity training and jet lag are linked to delayed sleep onset and reduced sleep efficiency. It reports that melatonin improves sleep onset latency in athletes, with mixed evidence on performance. It describes Z-drugs as useful only for short-term use because of tolerance and dependence risks, and CBD evidence as inconsistent and small in sample size. It presents CBT-I as more effective than medication in the long term, without quantified effect sizes.
paper.limitations: No review methods are described, and no effect sizes, sample sizes or evidence grades are reported for the main claims. Several citations do not match the claim they support: reference 79, a Norwegian football injury paper, is cited for doping and cannabis regulation, and reference 50, a commentary on poor quality control of over-the-counter melatonin, is cited for melatonin efficacy in athletes. A 2024 trimetazidine-contaminated melatonin supplement case is described without a citation. Several supporting studies are from non-athlete populations, for example aviators for zolpidem (ref 55) and general adults.
paper.practicalImplications: Start with behavioural measures for athlete insomnia, including CBT-I, sleep hygiene and scheduling hard sessions earlier in the day. Use medication only for short periods under medical supervision, and choose third-party tested melatonin products because of contamination and doping risk.
paper.athleteDev: Treat poor sleep caused by late training, travel, stress or overtraining as a recovery problem. Address it first with behavioural strategies such as CBT-I and sleep hygiene, and use short-term medication only under medical oversight. Check that any supplement is third-party tested.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. Return to sport, rehabilitation and injury management are not addressed as a decision pathway; injury and pain appear only as causes of sleep disruption, so the review cannot inform clearance or medication decisions after injury.

records.sourceFile: Post game recovery of isometric hamstring strength in a high risk hamstring strain injury group throughout an Australian Football League season.pdf

paper.citation: Sutherland T, Heasman J, Rogalski B, Fahey-Gilmour J, Peeling P. Post-game recovery of isometric hamstring strength in a high-risk hamstring strain injury group throughout an Australian Football League season. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022.
paper.abstract: This study examined post-game recovery of isometric hamstring strength in AFL players classed by the club as high risk for hamstring strain injury across a season. The test showed good inter-session reliability in pre-season, and linear mixed models linked a larger post-game strength decrement to a greater within-week strength change. The authors suggest early individual post-game testing could help inform hamstring recovery.
paper.tldr: In AFL players at high hamstring injury risk, post-game isometric hamstring strength loss was followed by within-week recovery, with the pattern varying by player. Early individual testing may help flag slower recovery, but the study does not set thresholds or link results to injury.
paper.methods: Part A tested reliability of an externally fixed isometric knee flexion test (45 degrees hip, 30 degrees knee flexion) in 16 players over three pre-season sessions. Part B tested 26 players twice a week (an initial test on the medical screening day and a re-test before the main training session) across 16 weeks of the 2021 season, combined with GPS and match statistics, and analyzed 21 players with both tests using linear mixed-effects models with player as a random effect.
paper.findings: Inter-session reliability was good (ICC 0.81 to 0.88, CV 6.73 to 7.33%). Post-game strength decrement was associated with within-week strength change (estimate -0.69, 95% CI -0.89 to -0.49, P<0.001), and the interaction with two or more days post-game (estimate 0.43, P<0.001) weakened that slope. Contested possessions were linked to a smaller post-game decrement (estimate 3.86, P=0.02); in the third model, relative sprint distance above 75% (estimate 2.71, P=0.022) and coming off an interstate AFL game (estimate 7.62, P=0.029) were linked to a larger within-week change.
paper.limitations: Testing was possible in only 16 of 23 season weeks because of COVID-19 restrictions, and only 21 of 26 players met the Part B inclusion rule. The club-selected high-risk group, skewed toward younger players, limits generalization to a whole squad, and the Discussion says the travel effect lacks confidence. The abstract calls the reliability inter-tester, but Methods describe inter-session reliability; the text gives a model 2 MAE of 6.78% where Table 4 gives 6.55; and the travel CI is 0.08 to 14.44 in the text but 0.8 to 14.44 in Table 5.
paper.practicalImplications: Early post-game isometric hamstring testing could help staff see which players lose more strength after a game and how much they regain within the week. The authors interpret the interaction as showing that players with a large decrement two or more days post-game have less capacity to regain strength later in the week, which supports testing early. The study sets no cut-offs and reports large between-player differences, so results should be read against each player's own baseline.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure performance outcomes. Its findings relate to recovery monitoring after match play and do not show that hamstring testing improves performance.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-play clearance. It defines no threshold for readiness and reports no injury outcomes, so it supports only individual monitoring of post-game strength change.

records.sourceFile: Post-match recovery of eccentric knee flexor strength in male professional football players.pdf

paper.citation: Bueno CA, Ribeiro-Alvares JBA, Oliveira GS, Grazioli R, Veeck F, Pinto RS, et al. Post-match recovery of eccentric knee flexor strength in male professional football players. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2021;47:140-146.
paper.abstract: This quasi-experimental study tracked eccentric knee flexor strength in 15 professional male footballers before a friendly match and at 0, 48 and 72 h after it. Strength fell 12% immediately after the match and was still 6% below baseline at 48 h. At 72 h the group mean was similar to baseline, but individual recovery varied, with 40% of players not fully recovered.
paper.tldr: After a professional friendly match, group eccentric hamstring strength fell 12% and was near baseline at 72 h, but 40% of players were still not fully recovered. The authors suggest individual monitoring after matches, which group averages would miss.
paper.methods: Quasi-experimental, single-group study in one club with 15 players who played at least 80 minutes in one of two friendly matches late in preseason. Eccentric knee flexor strength was the peak force across three Nordic hamstring exercise repetitions, measured on a custom two-load-cell device. Repeated-measures ANOVA with Fisher LSD post hoc tests was used, and each player was classed as fully recovered if the deficit was below the test coefficient of variation (about 5%).
paper.findings: Strength fell 12% immediately after the match (d=1.10, P=0.001) and was 6% below baseline at 48 h (d=0.57, P=0.011). At 72 h the group mean was 3.5% below baseline, which was not significant (d=0.34, P=0.122). Six of 15 players (40%) were fully recovered (deficit under 5%) at 48 h and nine (60%) at 72 h, and two players (13%) were still 'not recovered' at 72 h, with deficits larger than the 14% minimal detectable change.
paper.limitations: Only one club and 15 players were studied in friendly matches, and the authors state that the sample is small and external validity is limited. The 72 h result was not significant, which does not establish equivalence with baseline. Sleep, hydration, diet and match workload were not recorded, and post-match testing was staggered by up to 10 minutes.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could monitor each player's eccentric hamstring strength after matches, because the group mean hid incomplete recovery in 40% of players at 72 h. The authors suggest that individual recovery status should inform training load and the timing of the next match, including caution when a match falls within 72 h. The study did not link strength deficits to injury, so this is a monitoring suggestion rather than a validated injury-prevention protocol.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured eccentric hamstring strength, not performance. It does not show whether the 48 to 72 h deficits affect sprinting, match performance or training quality.
paper.rtp: The players were healthy and no return-to-play outcomes were measured, so the study cannot set clearance criteria after injury. The 5% and 14% thresholds were used only to classify recovery after matches and should not be used as return-to-play standards.

records.sourceFile: Postmatch Recovery Practices Carried Out in Professional Football - A Survey of 56 Portuguese Professional Football Teams.pdf

paper.citation: Querido SM, Brito J, Figueiredo P, Carnide F, Vaz JR, Freitas SR. Postmatch Recovery Practices Carried Out in Professional Football: A Survey of 56 Portuguese Professional Football Teams. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Practitioners from 56 Portuguese professional football teams completed an online questionnaire on postmatch recovery methods. Use of several methods differed across the 72 hours after matches and between home and away matches, and lower use after away matches was reported for most methods. The authors conclude that recovery methods are not applied uniformly across postmatch periods and that practice may need to be checked against the evidence on timing.
paper.tldr: Portuguese professional football teams used recovery methods differently across the 72 hours after home and away matches, with lower use after away matches for most methods. Nutrition and sleep were the most important and most used methods. The survey describes practice and does not test whether the methods work.
paper.methods: Online questionnaire of 19 questions (Portuguese, with an unvalidated English translation) completed by one practitioner per team in early 2020. Frequency of use was rated on a 5-point Likert scale for three postmatch periods after home and away matches, and methods were ranked for importance. Analyses used Friedman tests with Wilcoxon post hoc tests (Bonferroni, P < .017) and Wilcoxon tests for home versus away (P < .05), with effect sizes r.
paper.findings: Respondents were fitness coaches, physiotherapists, team physicians, head coaches and nurses, and half had more than five years of experience. Sleep was ranked most important and nutrition second, with the order reversed for frequency of use. After home matches, active recovery (r = .46), electrostimulation (r = .33), massage (r = .30) and stretching (r = .36) were used more often at 12-24 h than immediately after (P < .017). Immediately after home matches, active recovery, cold-water immersion, massage and stretching were used more than after away matches, and compression garments were used more after away matches (r = .27, P < .05).
paper.limitations: The sample is Portuguese only, so the findings may not generalise, and congested fixture periods were not examined. Frequency was not broken down by dose, intensity or duration of each method. The reported correlation between importance and usage (r = 1.00, P < .01, Results) is computed on summed rank points across nine methods, and a perfect rank correlation is inconsistent with Table 1, where sleep and nutrition swap the top two positions. The English questionnaire is unvalidated, although the Portuguese version was described as previously validated.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest cold-water immersion use in later postmatch periods may need to be reduced, since the evidence they cite favours use immediately after the match, and they call for research on why active recovery is used mostly at 12-72 h despite low cited effectiveness. They also recommend paying particular attention to recovery after away matches, when use was lower, especially after trips longer than four hours (68% of respondents said they change methods when travel exceeds 4 hours).
paper.athleteDev: The survey does not measure performance. It describes what teams report using after matches, with nutrition and sleep as the most used and most important methods, and it cannot show which timing or method improves performance.
paper.rtp: The survey covers postmatch recovery in the 72 hours after matches and does not study injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Potential role of cannabidiol on sports recovery - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Rojas-Valverde D. Potential Role of Cannabidiol on Sports Recovery: A Narrative Review. Frontiers in Physiology. 2021;12:722550.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of the evidence on cannabidiol (CBD) as a possible aid to recovery from exercise-related fatigue and muscle damage in sport. The author discusses CBD's proposed anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, analgesic, sleep, mood and anxiolytic actions and the prevalence of CBD use among athletes. The author concludes that the evidence is promising but not conclusive, with gaps in knowledge of the physiological pathways involved.
paper.tldr: This narrative review finds the evidence for CBD in sports recovery promising but not conclusive. It reports no evidence directly testing CBD for sports recovery and identifies a lack of studies in elite athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative review of preclinical and clinical literature on CBD and recovery-related outcomes such as inflammation, pain, sleep and mood. The author states the review followed the SANRA scale for narrative reviews but describes no systematic search or explicit inclusion criteria.
paper.findings: The author reports no evidence directly exploring CBD for sports recovery. Proposed effects (anti-inflammatory, analgesic, sleep-related, anxiolytic) rest mainly on preclinical work and clinical studies in patients. Human data cited include sedation at 300-400 mg and cortisol changes at 300 mg, and the author describes the sleep and mood evidence as promising but not specific to athletes.
paper.limitations: The author notes the review lacks explicit selection criteria and that a systematic review would present the evidence more clearly. Evidence in elite athletes is lacking, and the dose, frequency, timing and sex or level differences remain unknown. The review also cites CBD products that contain significant THC and notes that labels can be misleading.
paper.practicalImplications: The review does not support a recommended CBD dose, timing or frequency for athletes. Because some CBD products contain THC, and the author warns of a high risk of positive doping tests, staff should not assume product labels are accurate about THC content. Any use should be treated as unproven for recovery, and the review argues for controlled trials before guidance is given.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not show that CBD improves athletic performance; it says the performance evidence is unclear and that no athlete-specific trials are available. It can inform a discussion of a recovery aid with unproven benefit and doping risk, not a performance prescription.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport or injury rehabilitation, and it does not show that CBD reduces pain or soreness in injured athletes. Its pain and soreness content comes mainly from clinical and preclinical studies in patients, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Precovery vs recovery - Understanding the role of cherry juice in exercise recovery.pdf

paper.citation: McHugh MP. "Precovery" versus recovery: Understanding the role of cherry juice in exercise recovery. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2022.
paper.abstract: Cherry juice is a standard recovery drink for athletes. This narrative review reports 15 trials that measured muscle function, soreness or inflammation after exercise. The author concludes that muscle function recovers faster when juice is taken for several days before exercise, that soreness and systemic inflammation effects are more equivocal, and that tart cherry powder did not enhance recovery.
paper.tldr: Cherry juice appears to protect muscle function after exercise mainly when it is taken for several days before the exercise, not only on the day of or after it. Soreness and inflammation results are less consistent, and tart cherry powder showed no benefit in this review.
paper.methods: Fifteen of 19 cited cherry studies were selected by five criteria: a randomized human trial, a placebo control, at least one recovery measure (MVC or CMJ, soreness or CRP), an exercise insult sufficient to impair function or raise soreness or CRP, and measures at 1 and 2 days after exercise. No database search is described. The author calculated an index of protection at 24 and 48 h by comparing the change in the control and cherry conditions.
paper.findings: Of the 11 studies with an adequate exercise insult and a function measure, eight showed enhanced MVC or CMJ recovery. The average index of protection was 34 +/- 30% (MVC, 24 h) and 48 +/- 35% (CMJ, 24 h), and soreness was 29 +/- 18% across 14 studies at 24 h. CRP showed significant protection in two of eight studies, and the author finds no consistent difference in dose, timing or mode between the three soreness-protective studies and the ten without protection.
paper.limitations: The review states its selection criteria but describes no database search, and its index of protection is the author's own calculation. The author is a co-author of at least two included trials (Connolly et al. 2006; Howatson et al. 2010), and the abstract's word 'uniformly' overstates the review's own tally, since Lamb et al. found no benefit after 4 days of pre-exercise concentrate. Included studies averaged about 10 participants (range 8 to 16).
paper.practicalImplications: The review supports taking at least one serving a day for several days before a planned exercise insult, rather than starting on the day of or after exercise. Fresh-frozen juice and concentrate showed the most consistent function benefit, and tart cherry powder did not. The review states that no conclusion can be reached on continuing juice after exercise, so the author's advice to keep juice going through a season is the author's judgment, not a tested finding.
paper.athleteDev: Staff planning cherry juice for performance recovery can use a multi-day pre-exercise schedule rather than a post-event-only plan. The review supports this for muscle function, not for soreness or inflammation, so juice should not be promoted as a soreness fix.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport, injured athletes or return-to-play decisions. Its exercise insults were induced exercise such as eccentric, cycling, running and simulated sport work, so it cannot guide clearance or rehabilitation timing.
